translations.title: There are countries I remember...
translations.text:
There are countries I remember

as I remember my childhoods.

They are countries of sea or river,

of pastures, meadows, and waters.

My village beside the Rhône,

surrendered to river and cicadas;

Antilles in green-black palms

that lie halfway out to sea and call me;

Lig urian rock of Portofino,

Italian sea, Italian sea!


They have brought me to a country without rivers,

lands of Hagar, lands without water;

white Saras and red Saras,

where other races sinned,

with the red sin of the Atreids

that slashed clays recount;

that were not born like a child

with plump little bodies,

when I hear them, without a whistle,

when I cross them, without a glance.


I want to return to childhood lands;

carry me to a gentle country of waters.

Let me grow old in great pastures

and make the river fable upon fable.

Let a spring be my mother,

and let me seek her at siesta,

and let sweet water descend in jars

from a crag, sharp and rough.


May the fierce, icy water

overcome me and stop my breath.

May it break my cup, and as I drink,

make my insides young again!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Earth
translations.text:
Indian child, if you are tired,
lie down upon the Earth,
and just the same, if you are glad,
my child, play with her…

Wonderful things are heard
at the Indian drum of the Earth:
you hear the fire rise and fall,
seeking the sky, never at rest.
Round and round, you hear the rivers
in cascades beyond counting.
You hear the animals bellow;
you hear the axe devour the forest.
You hear Indian looms ringing.
You hear threshing, you hear feasts.

Where the Indian calls to it,
the Indian drum answers him,
and sounds near, and sounds far,
like one who flees and returns…

It takes all, it carries all
on the holy back of the Earth:
what walks, what sleeps,
what romps and what suffers;
it carries the living and the dead,
the Indian drum of the Earth.

When I die, do not weep, child:
press your breast against hers,
and if you hold your breath
as though you were everything or nothing,
you will hear her arm rise,
the arm that held me and gives me back,
and the mother who was broken
you will see made whole again.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: You shall love beauty, the shadow of God over the Universe...
translations.text:
I. You shall love beauty, which is God's shadow over the Universe.

II. There is no godless art. Even if you do not love the Creator, you will affirm Him by creating in His likeness.

III. You shall not offer beauty as bait for the senses, but as the soul's natural nourishment.

IV. It shall be no pretext for lust or vanity, but a divine practice.

V. You shall not seek it at fairs or take your work there, for Beauty is a virgin, and the one at fairs is not She.

VI. It shall rise from your heart into your song, and first it will have purified you.

VII. Your beauty shall also be called mercy, and shall console the hearts of men.

VIII. You shall give your work as you give a child: taking blood from your heart.

IX. Beauty shall not be a sleep-inducing opiate, but generous wine that fires you to action; for if you cease to be man or woman, you cease to be an artist.

X. From every creation you shall emerge ashamed, for it was less than your dream, and less than God's wondrous dream, which is Nature.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Guardian Angel
translations.text:
It is true, it is no tale;
there is a Guardian Angel
who takes you and carries you like the wind,
and goes with children wherever they go.

His hair is soft,
blowing in the breeze;
his eyes are sweet and grave,
they soothe you with a glance
and kill fear by giving light.
(It is no tale, it is true.)

His body, hands, and feet are wings;
the six wings fly or glide,
the six bear you on their beaten air,
and carry you just the same asleep.

He makes the ripe pulp sweeter
that you crush between greedy lips;
he breaks the walnut's sly shell
and saves you from gnomes and witches.

He helps you cut the roses
seated in traps of thorns;
he guides you over treacherous waters
and leads you up the steepest hills.

And though he walks beside you,
like one red cherry beside another,
when sin makes its sign to you
he gathers your soul and leaves your body.

It is true, it is no tale;
there is a Guardian Angel
who takes you and carries you like the wind,
and goes with children wherever they go.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: My little box...
translations.text:
I

My little box
from Olinalá,
rosewood,
jacaranda.

When I open it
it suddenly gives
its scent, fit for
the Queen of Sheba.

Ah, what a breath,
tropical: clove,
mahogany
and copal!

I set it here,
I leave it there;
along the corridors
it comes and goes.

It boils with patterns
like a country:
nopal, deer,
quail,

volcanoes
with towering necks,
and the Indian, airy
as the corn.

This is how they paint it,
just so, just so,
with Indian fingers
or hummingbird's;

and this is how
a masterful
Aztec hand makes it,
a quetzal hand.

II

When night
is drawing near,
so it may guard me
from its harm,

I place it
beneath my head,
where others put
their treasure.

Lovely dreams
it makes me dream;
it makes me laugh,
it makes me weep:

hand in hand
we cross the sea,
twin mountain ranges,
fields to plow.

Anáhuac
shines bright;
the beast Ajusco
is poised to leap,

and by the road
that leads toward the sea,
one goes to meet
Quetzalcoatl.

She is my breath,
I am her walk;
she is knowledge,
I am delirium.

And we stop,
like manna,
where the road
ends in abundance,

where the women
of Olinalá
shout to us: “Halalá!”
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Encounter
translations.text:
I found him on the path.
The water did not disturb its dream,
nor did the roses open wider;
amazement opened my soul.
And a poor woman has
a face full of tears!

He carried a light song
in his careless mouth,
and when he looked at me
the song he sang turned grave.
I looked at the path; it seemed
strange, as if dreamed.
And in the diamond dawn
my face was wet with tears.

He went on singing
and carried my gaze away…
Behind him the sages
were no bluer or taller.
No matter! In the air
my soul was left trembling.
Though no one has wounded me,
my face is wet with tears!

Tonight he has not kept vigil
beside the lamp as I have;
since he does not know, my longing
does not prick his narcissus breast;
yet perhaps through his dream
will pass the scent of broom,
for a poor woman
has a face full of tears!

I walked alone and feared nothing;
hungry and thirsty, I did not weep;
since I saw him pass,
my God has clothed me in wounds.
My mother prays for me
on her bed, her prayer trusting.
But perhaps forever
my face will be wet with tears!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The House
translations.text:
The table, child, is laid
in the still whiteness of cream,
and blue glints shimmer
on four walls of pottery.
This is the salt, this the oil,
and in the middle the Bread that almost speaks.
Gold lovelier than the Bread's gold
is in neither fruit nor broom;
its scent of grain and oven
brings joy that never sates.
We break it together, little one,
with hard fingers and soft palm,
and you gaze, amazed,
at black earth yielding a white flower.

Lower your eating hand,
your mother lowers hers too.
The wheat, child, belongs to air,
to sun, and to the hoe;
but this Bread, “God's own face,”
never reaches the tables of homes.
If other children have none,
better, my child, do not touch it;
better not take it with hands
that hang their heads in shame.

Hunger, grimacing,
whirls the threshing floors;
Bread and hunchback Hunger
seek one another and never meet.
If it should enter now to find it,
let us leave the Bread till morning;
let the burning fire mark the door,
which the Quechua Indian never closed.
Let us watch Hunger eat,
then sleep, body and soul!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Do not press my hands...
translations.text:
Do not press my hands.
The lasting time will come
to rest beneath much dust
and shadow in the woven fingers.

And you would say: “I cannot
love her, for her fingers have crumbled
like harvested sheaves.”

Do not kiss my mouth.
The moment will come, full
of fading light, when I shall have no lips
upon the damp earth.

And you would say: “I loved her, but I cannot
love her now, when she no longer breathes
the broom's scent from my kiss.”

I would be anguished to hear you,
and you would speak, mad and blind,
while my hand lies on your brow
when my fingers break,
and my breath descends upon your face
full of longing.

So do not touch me. I would lie
if I said I gave you my love
in these outstretched arms,
in my mouth, my neck;
and you, believing you drank it all,
would deceive yourself like a blind child.

For my love is not only this sheaf,
reluctant and weary, of my body,
that trembles at the touch of haircloth
and lags behind me in every flight.

It is what lies in the kiss, not the lip;
what breaks the voice, not the breast: it is
God's wind, passing through me, cleaving
the branch of my flesh, a wanderer!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Nocturne
translations.text:
Our Father in heaven,
why have You forgotten me?
You remembered the fruit in February,
when its ruby pulp was wounded.
My side too lies open,
yet You will not look toward me!

You remembered the dark cluster
and gave it to the crimson press;
you scattered the poplar leaves
with your breath in the delicate air.
In death's wide winepress
you still will not crush my breast!

Walking, I saw the violets open;
I drank the wind's Falernian wine,
and went down, my eyelids yellow,
so as to see no more January or April.

I clenched my mouth, flooded
with the stanza I shall never wring out…
You wounded the autumn cloud
yet will not turn toward me!

The one who kissed my cheek betrayed me;
he denied me for my shabby tunic.
In my verses I gave my face bloodied
as You gave Yours upon the cloth.
In my night in the Garden,
John was cowardly, the Angel hostile.

At last infinite weariness
has driven nails into my eyes: weariness
of the dying day and the dawn to come;
of the tin-gray sky and the indigo sky!

Now I loosen the martyr's sandal
and unbraid my hair, asking for sleep.
Lost in the night, I raise
the cry I learned from You:
Our Father in heaven,
why have You forgotten me?
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Amado Nervo, gentle profile, smiling lip...
translations.text:
Amado Nervo, gentle profile, smiling lip;
Amado Nervo, stanza and heart at peace: while I write,
a stone lies on your brow, your shroud descends
in immense snow, and terrible whiteness fell upon your face.

You wrote to me: “I am sad as the solitary,
but I have clothed my trembling in calm: the dreadful anguish
of shroud and charnel, the living longing
for Jesus Christ, my Lord.”

To think no hive will yield your sweetness,
that among tongues of hate you were a tongue of peace;
the rocking song of sorrow is departing,
there will be tribulation and you will not answer!

Day rose where you sang. A hundred nights
I slept in peace with your verse. I was still heroic,
still strong, because I still had you; your radiance
fell above the confusion. Now you are silent, dust, no more!

I never saw you. I shall not. My God has willed it.
Who joined your hands? Who, voice broken, said
the prayer of the dead beside your bed?
Who gave your eyes the astonishment of God?

I have days still beneath the suns. When shall I see you,
where find you and give you my grief: beneath the trembling
Southern Cross, or beyond, where winds fall silent,
where my heart, impure, cannot reach?

Remember me, sad dust and ashes,
when you are in your kingdom of ecstatic sapphire.
Cry out, beneath God's shade, what you knew: we are orphans,
we walk alone, you saw us; all flesh begs in anguish to die!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Questions
translations.text:
How do suicides lie sleeping, Lord?
A clot at the mouth, both temples emptied,
the moons of their eyes pale and enlarged,
hands turned toward an invisible anchor?

Or do You come after the people have gone,
lower the lid over the blinded eye,
set the entrails right without pain or sound,
and cross their hands over the silent breast?

Does the rosebush the living water over their grave
paint its roses in the shape of wounds?
Is its scent sharp, its beauty dark,
its thinned branches woven with serpents?

Answer me, Lord: when the soul escapes
through the wet door of long wounds,
does it enter Your realm, cleaving the calm air,
or do maddened wings crackle?

Does a narrow, livid ring close around it?
Is the ether a field flowering with monsters?
In terror do they fail even to find Your name?
Or do they cry over Your sleeping heart?

Will no ray of sun reach them one day?
No water wash them of their red stigmata?
Is Your womb cold for them alone,
Your keen ear deaf, Your eyes shut tight?

So man claims, in error or malice;
but I, who have tasted You like wine, Lord,
while others call You Justice,
shall call You nothing but Love!

I know that man was always a hard claw,
the cataract a vertigo, the mountain roughness.
You are the vessel where all garden nectars
on Earth's orchards swell with sweetness!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Desolation
translations.text:
Dense, eternal mist, so I may forget where
the brine wave of the sea cast me ashore.
The land I came to has no spring;
it has a long night that hides me like a mother.

The wind circles my house with sobs
and cries, and breaks my shout like glass.
On the white plain, whose horizon has no end,
I watch intense, painful sunsets die.

Whom can she call, who has come this far,
when only the dead have gone farther?
They alone behold a silent, lifeless sea
growing between their arms and their loved ones' arms!

The ships, their sails white in the harbor,
come from lands where none of mine are;
their fair-eyed men know not my rivers,
and bring pale fruit without my orchards' light.

The question rising to my throat
falls back defeated as I watch them pass:
they speak strange tongues, not the moved tongue
my poor mother sings in lands of gold.

I watch the snow descend like dust on a grave;
the mist grow like one who is dying;
and, lest I go mad, I cannot find the moments,
for the long night has only just begun.

I gaze at the entranced plain and gather its grief,
which comes to see the mortal landscapes.
Snow is the face appearing at my windows:
its whiteness will always descend from heaven!

Always it, silent as God's great gaze upon me;
always its blossom over my house; always,
like fate that neither wanes nor passes,
it will descend to cover me, terrible and entranced.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Crazy Old Carnival
translations.text:
Crazy old Carnival
sold his mattress
to buy bread and wine,
spaghetti and sausage.

Like a glutton he ate
a mountain of fried cakes;
his belly grew so big
it looked like a balance scale.
He drank and drank, and his face
turned red.
His belly burst;
he ate, ate, and would not stop.

Shrove Tuesday ends Carnival,
and they hold his funeral,
for from dust he was born
and to dust he will return.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Stay!
translations.text:
Stay! Rest
beside me.
Do not go.
I will always care for you.
You will regret everything
except coming to me,
freely, proudly.
I love you. I have no thought
that is not of you;
I carry no desire in my blood
that is not for you.
You know it.
I see no other companion in my life,
no other joy.
Stay.
Rest. Worry about nothing.
In my heart, sleep tonight.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The ineffable joy
translations.text:
Celebrate the great, ineffable joy
of living, of being young, of being strong,
of sinking eager white teeth
into earth's sweetest fruits;
of laying bold, knowing hands
upon all that is purest and most secret,
of drawing the bow against every quarry
that ravenous desire hunts.

To hear all the light music,
to behold, with blazing eyes,
the world's fair face, as a happy lover
looks upon his beloved.

To you, pleasure, my friend!
To you, dream!
I would clothe you in the reddest
of royal purples, even if its silk
were dyed with the blood of my veins.
I would crown you with white roses
so transfigured you might sing
of divine Joy, Joy, Joy,
magnificent, unconquerable!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: A Dream
translations.text:
She was dead; the wound, without warmth,
was scarcely visible in her side:
a narrow escape, for so much life!

The funeral cloth was no whiter
than the corpse. No human eye
will ever see a thing whiter than that white.

Impetuous Spring was burning.
At the panes, helpless gnats
beat with rustling wings…

Warmth fled her. I said: “Are you sleeping?”
With a savage, violent smile,
I asked again, closer: “Sleeping? Asleep?”

“Asleep?” Remembering that voice
was not mine, I stiffened with fear
and listened. Not a murmur, not a sound.

Captive in the red architecture,
a strong odor of an opened grave
spread in the heat.

Death's invisible breath
was choking me in the closed room.
To the motionless woman I said,
“Are you asleep? Asleep?” Nothing, nothing…
The funeral cloth was no whiter.
On the earth of men no eye
will see anything whiter than that white!…
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Vas spirituale
translations.text:
Her spiritual right hand upon a psalter,
solemn and taciturn,
a woman keeps watch in the mystery
of the night hour.

A great forest of symbols surrounds her.
Over her devout brow, flooded
with otherworldly brightness,
the temple's vast Gothic arches
cast their net. Winged powers
fill the broad shadowy naves;
on the white marble of tomb slabs
rest indolent statues, reclining
amid garlands of eternal roses.

Beside the burnished cedar doors
that guard the sanctuary's deathlike rest,
on friezes and moldings, fabulous
beasts mingle in hieratic poses.

Beneath the white of her stole
she meditates, white, alone,
solemn. She seems to embody
the three Theological Virtues;
zodiacal signs in a circle
halo her violet hair.

Feathers and gems of iridescent sheen
constellate her heavy robe;
her ringed, golden, spiritual right hand
rests on the instrument,
and at her feet a Latin pontiff
slowly and rhythmically swings
a fragile censer of fine gold.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Women
translations.text:
There have been serene women with clear eyes,
infinite and silent as the plain
a river of pure water crosses.

There have been women with glints of gold,
rivals of summer and fire, like lustful
wheat fields their teeth cannot wound the sickle,
but which burn within with sidereal fire
beneath the stripped sky.

There have been women so light
that a single word, one alone,
made them slaves. And there were others,
with reddish hands, who gently touched a brow
and dispelled terrible thoughts.

And others whose bloodless, supple hands,
with slow turns, seemed to insinuate themselves,
weaving a strange and delicate web
where veins appeared to be
threads vibrating ultramarine.

Pale women, withered, devastated,
burned in love's fire to their deepest selves,
their blazing faces consumed,
noses quivering with the impulse
of restless nostrils, lips parted
as if moving toward spoken words,
eyelids livid as violet petals.

And still there have been others, and,
wondrously, I have known them.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Boscán, you have been avenged, at my expense...
translations.text:
Boscán, you have been avenged, at my expense,

for my past harshness and my severity,

with which I used to reproach you for the tenderness

of your gentle heart.


Now I punish myself each day

for such wildness and such folly;

but it is a time when I might well blush

at my baseness and punish myself.


Know that, in my prime, and armed,

with my eyes open, I have surrendered

to the child you know, blind and naked.


No heart was ever consumed

by so beautiful a fire. If I am asked

about the rest, I am mute about the rest.
translations.review_note: Translated directly; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Neither the hateful French arms...
translations.text:
Neither the hateful French arms,

set against my angry breast,

nor, on the guarded walls with their defenses,

the poisoned shots and arrows;


neither the perilous skirmishes,

nor that fierce, imitated din

of what was made for Jupiter

by Vulcan's skillful hands,


could, though I offered myself

to the dangers of harsh war,

rob my fate of a single hour.


But a taint in the air, in a single day,

took me from the world and buried me in you;

I am here, so far from my homeland.
translations.review_note: Translated directly; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Sonnet XI
translations.text:
Beautiful nymphs, who dwell within the river,

content in homes built out of gleaming stones

and held aloft on columns made of glass,


whether you now weave, absorbed in your work,

or fashion delicate cloth,

or whether, set apart from one another,

you tell of loves and lives;


leave your work awhile, lift up

your golden heads to look at me,

and you will not detain yourselves long, as I fare,


for either pity will keep you from hearing me,

or, turned to water here by weeping,

you may console me there at leisure.
translations.review_note: Translated directly; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Beautiful nymphs, who dwell within the river...
translations.review_note: Translated directly; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Sonnet XXVII
translations.text:
Love, love, I put on a garment

cut from your cloth; when I first wore it, it was loose,

but grew tighter and close-fitting

once it was on me.


Ever since I consented to this,

such regret has seized me

that sometimes, in my anguish, I try

to tear apart what I have entered into.


But who can free himself from this garment,

when his nature is so opposed to it

that it has come to conform to it?


If some part of my reason remains,

it dares not show itself for my sake,

for amid such contradiction it is not safe.
translations.review_note: Translated directly; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Thinking the road ran straight...
translations.text:
Thinking the road ran straight,

I came to such misfortune

that I cannot imagine, even in madness,

anything that might satisfy me for a moment.


The open field seems narrow to me;

the clear night is dark;

sweet company, bitter and harsh,

and the bed, a hard field of battle.


Of sleep, if any comes, that part alone

which is the image of death

suits my weary soul.


In short, however things may be, I am so placed

that I already judge a less painful hour

by the one in which I saw what is a sword.
translations.review_note: Translated directly; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Daphne's arms had begun to grow...
translations.text:
Daphne's arms had begun to grow,

and turned, they showed themselves as long branches;

I saw the hair that darkened gold

become green leaves.


Rough bark covered

her tender limbs, still stammering;

her white feet sank into the earth

and changed to twisting roots.


He who caused such harm

by force of weeping made grow

the tree he watered with his tears.


O wretched state, O cruel fate!

For as he weeps for her, each day he makes

the cause and reason for his weeping grow.
translations.review_note: Translated directly; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: The foundation lies thrown to earth...
translations.text:
The foundation that sustained

my weary life lies thrown to earth.

Oh, how much good ends in a single day!

Oh, how many hopes the wind carries away!


Oh, how idle my thought becomes

when it concerns what might be good for me!

My torment punishes my hope,

as though it were barren, a thousand times.


Most often I surrender; at other times I resist

with such fury, with such new strength,

that I could break a mountain set upon me.


This is the desire that leads me

to wish to see again one day

the one it would have been better never to see.
translations.review_note: Translated directly; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: While rose and lily...
translations.text:
While rose and lily show their colors

in your face,

and while your ardent, honest gaze

sets the heart alight and reins it in;


and while your hair, drawn

from the vein of gold, with swift flight,

moves, scatters, and disorders the wind

over your lovely, upright white neck;


pluck the sweet fruit

from your joyful spring, before angry time

covers the lovely summit with snow.


The icy wind will make the rose wither;

swift age will change everything,

so as to change nothing of its custom.
translations.review_note: Translated directly; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Your image is written in my soul...
translations.review_note: Translated directly; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ode to the Flower of Gnido
translations.text:
Sonnet XXXII — I am with you, bathed in tears...

		I am with you, bathed in tears,
breaking the air always with
		sighs;
and it pains me more that I dare not tell you
that for your sake I have come
		to such a state,

		that seeing where I am and what I have traveled
along the narrow road of
		following you,
if I would turn back to flee you,
I faint at the sight of all
		I have left behind:
and
		if I would climb the lofty summit,
at every step on the way

		sad examples of those who have fallen terrify me.

		Above all, I now lack the light
of hope, by which I used to walk
		through the dark region of your forgetfulness.
translations.review_note: Translated directly; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Boscán, the arms and fury of Mars
translations.text:
Boscán, the arms and fury of Mars,
        which, watering African soil with its own blood,
        make the Roman empire
        flourish again in this land,


        have brought back to memory the skill
        and ancient valor of Italy,
        by whose might and valiant hand
        Africa trembled from end to end.


        Here, where the Roman blaze,
        where fire and its unbridled flame
        left Carthage only its name,


        love turns and turns my thoughts,
        wounds and kindles my fearful soul,
        and I dissolve in tears and ashes.
translations.note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review.

translations.title: I have left the sea and lands between
translations.text:
I have left sea and lands between myself
        and all the good I had, poor wretch;
        moving farther away each day,
        I have passed through peoples, customs, languages.


        I have lost hope of returning now;
        in my imagination I devise remedies,
        and the surest one I hope for is the day
        that will end both life and care.


        I could find relief from any ill
        by seeing you, my lady, or hoping to,
        if I could hope without losing that hope.


        But since I cannot see you to save myself,
        I find no remedy except to die;
        and if death is one, I cannot obtain it either.
translations.note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review.

translations.title: If, to restrain this desire
translations.text:
If, to restrain this desire,
        mad, impossible, vain, fearful,
        and to heal myself of so dangerous an ill
        as making myself believe what I do not believe,


        it does me no good to see myself as I am,
        either too bold or too afraid,
        in such confusion that I never dare
        entrust to myself the ill I harbor,


        what good will it do me to see the picture
        of him who, falling with melted wings,
        gave his fame and name to the sea,


        and of him who weeps for his fire and folly
        among those familiar trees,
        scarcely cooled in the water?
translations.note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review.

translations.title: Illustrious honor of the name of Cardona
translations.text:
Illustrious honor of the name of Cardona,
        tenth dweller on Parnassus,
        noble subject for an immortal crown
        to Tansillo, Minturno, and learned Tasso;


        if strength and spirit do not desert
        your Laso halfway along the road,
        for your sake my daring steps will carry me
        to the difficult summit of Helicon.


        Then with sweet song that checks the water's course,
        I shall be able, without toil, to lead
        along a path dry until now


        the famed, rich Tagus of my homeland,
        so that from the worth of its shining sands
        it may pay great tribute to your name.
translations.note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review.

translations.title: As brave Leander crossed the sea
translations.text:
As brave Leander crossed the sea,
        burning all over with the fire of love,
        the wind grew stronger, and the water
        raged with furious force.


        Worn down by his urgent struggle,
        unable to withstand the waves,
        and more distressed by the joy he lost in dying
        than by the loss of his own life,


        he raised his weary voice as best he could
        and spoke to the waves in this way,
        though they never heard his voice:


        “Waves, since you insist that I must die,
        let me reach her first, and on my return
        unleash your fury on my life.”
translations.note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review.

translations.title: I thank heaven that at last from my neck
translations.text:
I thank heaven that at last I have shaken
        the heavy yoke completely from my neck,
        and that from shore I shall watch the sea
        enraged by wind without fearing it.


        I shall see the life of the lover,
        absorbed in his error and lulled by his delusion,
        hanging by a slender hair,
        deaf to the voices that warn him of it.


        The ills of mortals will gladden me;
        yet my heart is not so inhuman
        in this error of mine as it may seem,


        for I rejoice as a healthy man does,
        not at seeing others suffer ills,
        but at seeing himself free of them.
translations.note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review.

translations.title: O executing fate in my sorrows...
translations.text:
O executing fate in my sorrows,
        how keenly I felt your rigorous laws!
        You cut the tree with hurtful hands,
        and scattered fruit and flowers upon the ground.


        In little space my loves lie fallen,
        and all the hope of all my things,
        turned into disdainful ashes,
        deaf to my complaints and cries.


        The tears that in this sepulcher
        are shed today and have been shed
        receive, though there they be of no avail to you,


        until that everlasting dark night
        closes these fair eyes of mine that saw you,
        leaving me with others who may see you.
translations.review_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review.

translations.title: My tongue goes where pain guides it
translations.text:
My tongue goes where pain guides it;
        I, with my pain, walk unguided;
        together we must go with sure intent;
        each goes to end where it would not.


        I, because I go with no companion
        except the one my folly makes for me;
        it, because it is led by him who came
        to make it say more than it would wish.


        And the law is so unequal for me
        that though it always knows me innocent,
        I always pay for another's fault as mine.


        What blame have I for my tongue's frenzy,
        if I am in such distress
        that suffering itself no longer knows me?
translations.review_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review.

translations.title: Mario, ungrateful love as witness
translations.text:
Mario, ungrateful love as witness
        to my pure faith and great steadfastness,
        showing in me its vile nature,
        which is to do greater wrong to the closest friend;


        fearing that if I write or speak
        of its nature, I diminish its greatness,
        its strength not sufficing for my harshness,
        it has strengthened the hand of my enemy.


        And so, in the part the right hand
        commands, and in that which declares
        the soul's conception, I was wounded.


        Yet I shall make this offense cost dearly
        to the offender, for now I am healed,
        free, desperate, and offended.
translations.review_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review.

translations.title: Julio, after I left in tears
translations.text:
Julio, after I left in tears
        the one from whom my thoughts never part,
        and left that part of my soul
        which gave the body life and strength,


        I take a strict account of my own good,
        and, being so afflicted, all good fails me,
        so that I fear in part
        even breath will fail me as I sigh;


        and with this fear my tongue tries
        to speak with you, O sweet friend,
        of that day's bitter memory,


        when I began, as witness,
        to be able to bring you news of your soul,
        and to learn from you of mine.
translations.review_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review.

translations.title: At the entrance to a valley, in a desert
translations.text:
At the entrance to a valley, in a wilderness
        where no one passed or could be seen,
        I saw a dog, strangely, making
        frantic gestures of pain and confusion;


        now it lets its lament fly to the open sky,
        now it tracks along the road;
        it walks, turns back, stops, and still
        lay fainting as if dead.


        His master had gone away from his sight,
        and he could not find him, and this he grieves;
        see how far the pain of absence reaches.


        His plight moved me to pity;
        I said to him, sore-hearted: Be patient,
        for I know reason, and I too am absent.
translations.review_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review.
